new_entities.name: Mediterranean diet in children
new_entities.description: A Mediterranean dietary pattern or intervention applied to children or adolescents, often emphasizing vegetables, legumes, fruit, olive oil, fish, and reduced ultra-processed foods.

new_entities.name: Growth outcomes
new_entities.description: Anthropometric outcomes such as BMI, weight, waist circumference, body fat, or healthy growth trajectories in children.

edges.effect_quant: A 2026 meta-analysis of 18 studies with 1539 participants found Mediterranean diet-based interventions improved BMI (ES 0.34, 95% CI 0.13-0.56) and body fat (ES 0.64, 95% CI 0.19-1.08) in children and adolescents with overweight or obesity.
edges.population: children and adolescents, especially those with overweight, obesity, or metabolic risk
edges.mechanism: Mediterranean dietary patterns may lower energy density, improve satiety and diet quality, reduce ultra-processed food intake, and support healthier body composition over time.
edges.summary: Mediterranean-style diet interventions in children tend to support healthier growth and body-composition outcomes overall, particularly in overweight or at-risk pediatric populations.
edges.caveats: Benefits are stronger in children with excess adiposity than in general-population samples. Many interventions combine Mediterranean diet counseling with physical activity or broader lifestyle support, so purely dietary effects are not always separable.

evidence.citation: Rosi A et al 2026 Nutr Rev
